title: Electrical Components & Measuring Instruments

notes.heading: 1. PMMC, Moving-Iron (MI) & Electrodynamometer Meters
notes.proseLatex: A Permanent-Magnet Moving-Coil (PMMC) instrument develops deflecting torque $T_d = NBIA \propto I$, giving a UNIFORM (linear) scale with eddy-current damping, and responds strictly to the AVERAGE (DC) value — pure sinusoidal AC produces zero net deflection! A Moving-Iron (MI) instrument develops $T_d = \frac{1}{2}I^2\frac{dL}{d\theta} \propto I^2$, giving a NON-LINEAR cramped scale (air-friction damped) that reads TRUE RMS on BOTH AC and DC! Electrodynamometers serve as standard wattmeters reading real average power $P = VI\cos\phi$.

keyFormulas.label: PMMC (Average) vs Moving-Iron (True RMS) Readings
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Predict exact PMMC vs MI readings on mixed DC + AC waveforms.

examples.problemLatex: Current $i(t) = 3 + 4\sqrt{2}\sin(100\pi t)\text{ A}$ passes through a PMMC ammeter in series with a Moving-Iron ammeter. Find both readings.
stepsLatex: PMMC reads average value over a cycle: $\langle i(t)\rangle = 3 + 0 = 3\text{ A}$.

notes.heading: 2. Ammeter Shunt, Voltmeter Multiplier & Ideal Meter Resistances
notes.proseLatex: An ideal ammeter has $R_A = 0\,\Omega$ (connected in series) and an ideal voltmeter has $R_V = \infty$ (connected in parallel). To extend a coil ($I_g, R_g$) to full-scale current $I = m I_g$, place a low manganin SHUNT $R_{\text{sh}} = \frac{R_g}{m - 1}$ in PARALLEL; to extend full-scale voltage from $V_g = I_g R_g$ to $V = m V_g$, place a high MULTIPLIER $R_s = (m - 1)R_g$ in SERIES. Voltmeter sensitivity is $S_V = \frac{1}{I_{\text{fsd}}}\;\Omega/\text{V}$ (higher $\Omega/\text{V}$ means LESS circuit loading error!).

keyFormulas.label: Parallel Shunt, Series Multiplier & Ω/V Sensitivity
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Design shunts and multipliers and compare voltmeter loading.

examples.problemLatex: Convert a $1\text{ mA},\; 50\,\Omega$ PMMC coil into a $0\text{--}10\text{ V}$ DC voltmeter.
stepsLatex: Full-scale coil drop $V_g = 10^{-3}\times 50 = 0.05\text{ V}$, so multiplying factor $m = 10 / 0.05 = 200$.

notes.heading: 3. Resistance Bridges (Wheatstone, Kelvin, Megger) & AC Bridges
notes.proseLatex: Medium resistances ($1\,\Omega\text{--}100\text{ k}\Omega$) use the Wheatstone bridge ($R_1 R_4 = R_2 R_3$ at null); LOW resistances ($< 1\,\Omega$) require Kelvin's double bridge to eliminate lead/contact resistance; and HIGH insulation resistances ($> 100\text{ k}\Omega$) use a Megger or loss-of-charge method. Standard AC bridges: Maxwell inductance-capacitance bridge ($L_1 = R_2 R_3 C_4$, medium-$Q$ coils), Hay's bridge (high-$Q$ coils), Schering bridge (capacitance & dielectric loss), and Wien bridge (frequency).

keyFormulas.label: Wheatstone & Maxwell Bridge Null Conditions
keyFormulas.latex: $\frac{R_1}{R_2} = \frac{R_3}{R_4}\;\text{(Wheatstone)},\qquad Z_1 Z_4 = Z_2 Z_3\;\text{(general AC bridge)}$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Select the right bridge for low/medium/high R, L, C, and frequency.

conceptPrimer.heading: PMMC vs Moving-Iron: What Each Meter Reads
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: A Permanent-Magnet Moving-Coil meter develops deflecting torque $T_d = NBIA \propto I$, so it reads the AVERAGE (DC component) of any waveform — a pure sinusoid gives zero net deflection, however large its amplitude. A Moving-Iron meter develops $T_d = \frac{1}{2}I^2\frac{dL}{d\theta} \propto I^2$ on both half-cycles, so it reads TRUE RMS on AC and DC alike, on a non-linear (cramped-at-start) scale. Micro-check: $i(t) = 2 + 3\sqrt{2}\sin(\omega t)$: PMMC reads $2\ \text{A}$, MI reads $\sqrt{2^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{13} \approx 3.61\ \text{A}$.

conceptPrimer.heading: Electrodynamometer and the Wattmeter
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: The electrodynamometer replaces the permanent magnet with two coils (fixed field + moving pressure coil); its torque depends on the product of the two currents, so with the current coil in series and the pressure coil across the load it indicates REAL average power $P = VI\cos\phi$ on either AC or DC. It is the standard for wattmeter calibration precisely because it reads true DC-equivalent power on AC. Micro-check: $V = 230\ \text{V}$, $I = 10\ \text{A}$, $\cos\phi = 0.8$: the wattmeter shows $230 \times 10 \times 0.8 = 1840\ \text{W}$.

conceptPrimer.heading: Shunts and Multipliers: Extending Meter Ranges
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Ideal ammeter: $R_A = 0$ (series connection — never across a source, or it shorts it). Ideal voltmeter: $R_V = \infty$ (parallel connection). To extend a coil ($I_g$, $R_g$) to $I = m I_g$, add a low manganin shunt $R_{\text{sh}} = \frac{R_g}{m-1}$ in PARALLEL; to extend $V_g = I_g R_g$ to $V = m V_g$, add a multiplier $R_s = (m-1)R_g$ in SERIES. Micro-check: $1\ \text{mA}$, $50\ \Omega$ coil as a $0$–$10\ \text{V}$ voltmeter: $V_g = 0.05\ \text{V}$, $m = 200$, $R_s = 199 \times 50 = 9950\ \Omega$.

conceptPrimer.heading: Voltmeter Sensitivity: the Ω/V Figure of Merit
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Voltmeter sensitivity $S_V = \frac{1}{I_{\text{fsd}}}\ \Omega/\text{V}$ counts how many ohms of internal resistance ride on every volt of range. A HIGHER $\Omega/\text{V}$ meter draws less current from the circuit, so it produces LESS loading error — the low-sensitivity voltmeter 'lies' on high-resistance dividers. Micro-check: a $1000\ \Omega/\text{V}$ meter on its $100\ \text{V}$ range has $R_V = 100\ \text{k}\Omega$; on a $100\ \text{k}\Omega$ source divider it halves the reading — pick the $1000\ \Omega/\text{V}$ meter.

conceptPrimer.heading: Resistance Bridges: Match the Range
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Wheatstone bridge ($R_1 R_4 = R_2 R_3$ at null, galvanometer as null detector) handles MEDIUM resistances ($1\ \Omega$–$100\ \text{k}\Omega$). Below $1\ \Omega$, lead and contact resistances corrupt Wheatstone — Kelvin's DOUBLE bridge removes them with a second ratio arm. Above $100\ \text{k}\Omega$ (insulation resistance), the Megger (hand-driven or electronic high-voltage ohmmeter) or loss-of-charge method applies. Micro-check: a $0.5\ \Omega$ shunt resistance goes to Kelvin, never plain Wheatstone.

conceptPrimer.heading: AC Bridges and Their Specialities
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Every AC bridge balances on $Z_1 Z_4 = Z_2 Z_3$ (both magnitude AND phase). Maxwell's inductance–capacitance bridge ($L_1 = R_2 R_3 C_4$) suits medium-$Q$ coils; Hay's bridge handles HIGH-$Q$ coils; Schering measures capacitance and dielectric loss (high-voltage cables, insulators); Wien bridge measures FREQUENCY ($f = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{R_1 R_2 C_1 C_2}}$, the RC oscillator heart). Micro-check: a coil with $Q > 10$ goes to Hay's, not Maxwell.

keyDefinitions.definition: Permanent-magnet moving-coil meter; deflecting torque $NBIA$; uniform scale, eddy-current damped, DC average only.
Meter whose torque $\propto I^2\frac{dL}{d\theta}$; reads true RMS on AC and DC; air-friction damped; cramped scale.
Two-coil instrument whose torque uses the product of coil currents; the standard wattmeter ($P = VI\cos\phi$).
Low manganin resistance in parallel with a PMMC coil to extend its current range ($R_{\text{sh}} = R_g/(m-1)$).
High resistance in series with a PMMC coil to extend its voltage range ($R_s = (m-1)R_g$).
$\Omega/\text{V}$ figure $= 1/I_{\text{fsd}}$; higher sensitivity means smaller circuit loading.
Reading shift caused by the meter drawing current from the measured circuit (worst for low-$\Omega/\text{V}$ voltmeters).
Modified Wheatstone with a second ratio arm that cancels lead/contact resistance; for resistances below $1\ \Omega$.
High-voltage insulation tester for resistances above $\sim 100\ \text{k}\Omega$.
Mechanism (eddy-current for PMMC, air-friction for MI) that brings the pointer to rest quickly without oscillation.

mcqSelfTest.explanation: PMMC reads the DC average $= 2\ \text{A}$; MI reads true RMS $= \sqrt{2^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{13} \approx 3.61\ \text{A}$.

More $\Omega/\text{V}$, less lie: sensitivity fights loading error.
Ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel — reversed, the ammeter shorts.
Kelvin below one ohm, Megger above hundred k.

commonMistakes: Expecting a PMMC meter to show RMS on AC (it shows the average — zero for pure AC).
Using $\sqrt{2}$-scaled peak twice: RMS of DC + AC is $\sqrt{I_0^2 + I_m^2/2}$.
Claiming a lower $\Omega/\text{V}$ voltmeter is better (it loads the circuit more).
Measuring sub-ohm resistances with a plain Wheatstone bridge.
Forgetting that MI works on DC too (it reads RMS there as well).
Connecting an ammeter across a supply 'to measure the voltage'.
Breaking a balanced bridge by swapping supply and galvanometer — it stays balanced.
examChecklist: Decide DC-average (PMMC) vs true-RMS (MI) before any waveform question.
Convert $I_g R_g$ to $V_g$ first; find $m$; then apply the shunt/multiplier formula.
State the shunt connection (parallel) and multiplier connection (series).
Quote sensitivity in $\Omega/\text{V}$ and link it to loading error.
Map resistance magnitude to Kelvin / Wheatstone / Megger.
Recite the AC-bridge roster: Maxwell, Hay's, Schering, Wien.
Use $Z_1 Z_4 = Z_2 Z_3$ for any AC-bridge balance.
Never place an ammeter in parallel with a source.
